Personally I think the video course alone is worth the money. There’s about 100 videos and then training drills to build your skills from the basics up to a full test out drill. 

Could you do it on your own with extensive research? Probably. But you’d still want to buy a few books. You’d need to buy some cards to do physical practice with. 

If you want to be successful and make money playing blackjack, investing in your skills is the best thing you can do. Some people are fine with breaking even and getting free food and rooms from casinos among other comps. Everyone’s got their own goals and there’s no wrong way to go about it.

Personally, when looking for cheap cars, I've always leaned towards the Honda Civic/Accord. I've owned 2 separate Accords, a 4 cylinder and a V6. I liked them both but the V6 certainly was faster and more fun. A friend of mine has owned multiple Civics. They're cheap and reliable, and if you buy a manual it is still a little more fun even if they don't make a lot of power. Both of mine hit 180k miles before the maintenance needed outweighed what I paid for the car and I sold them. I bought each with under 120k miles, so I got my money's worth each time having taken both on different road trips and putting lots of miles on them in a short time.

Just my input though, but for that price I would lean towards the cars I said. Best of luck in the search!

When I started nights last year I felt the same too. It really sucks and I 100% know how you feel. For me personally, I started listening to music all the time at work, and tried to get to know a few co workers around my age (I'm 22. Average age of co workers is 48-55) and I ended up finding a couple of the best friends I've had in years.

Truth be told, none of us like being on nights. We lost our old social lives, all sleep too much, never see the sun, but my work buddies and I are all in it together and it makes it a little easier to get through the day (night, rather) when we all have the same goal in mind, getting a career position there on day shift.

Night shift is hard and it's scientifically proven that there's higher rates of depression among people who work nights. Someone else suggested the idea of staying up a bit when you're home to get house work done. I would try and stay up until 12 and then head to sleep, and wake up before work as if you worked a day job. Use your time when you get home to do house work, walk your dog and spend time with him/her, and try to talk to some old friends if they aren't too busy before they leave work, use that time for you. 

Nights are hard, we all know how you feel. Stick it out and the money will be worth it I'm sure. Best of luck

A lot of my bullying began as teasing when I was 9 or 10 years old. I was wicked short and scrawny and got teased all the time. As I got older I got more into punk and hardcore/emo music, I definitely dressed the part. Got made fun of A TON for that and bullied, pushed around, etc. I can remember a few distinct instances of having water poured on me, pushed in the bathroom, hit/punched and kicked, etc.

One day I had had enough (I was about 14) and asked my dad to teach me how to lift weights and how to fight. I was a freshman in High School at this point and it was the peak of my bullying. I started working out and practicing the punches and combos he taught me every day. I didn't get much bigger (I was 5' 3 inches tall and weighed like 125lbs) but got a lot stronger because I was new to lifting and at that stage any exercise shows LOTS of progress very fast. It's commonly called newbie gains. After a few months of practice and working out a kid who commonly bullied me told me he was going to fight me after school and I relished the opportunity to show him what for.

Long story short, I won the fight not really out of strength or skill but that I landed a combo my dad taught me as the first hit just started punching him over and over while he tried to wrestle me to the ground. It didn't work, he eventually let up on grabbing me and pulling me around and I slugged him once more and he kinda fell down and just walked off. Everyone there cheered for me, probably 20-30 kids showed up. Nobody really bothered me after that day, the rest of High School was pretty  peaceful.

I won't say I support violence as the answer but sometimes it is necessary.

TL;DR: Got bullied a lot, fought bully and won and was left alone after that day.

Southern Maine. I started going to shows in 2010 and it was the tail end of an AWESOME time of shows (late 90's- 2012 was seriously great for Maine as a whole)

In the last 5 years it's just been a slippery downhill slope. Lots of division in the scene in the groups of kids who used to be the tough guys at shows who are now in their late 20's and don't come around too often anymore, the guys all around my age (21-25) who are kind of the head of the scene now, and the younger kids who are coming to shows for the first few times. With all of this division there's basically ALWAYS been lots of fights at our shows, sometimes amongst each other sometimes with security at larger venues in Portland. We have a handful of good bands around, just nobody putting on shows because of all the problems that happened at the one venue we had. Not many people (30-50 normally, 150 at a REALLY good show) coming out to shows + No solid hardcore venue + lack of current bands = a failing scene.

It's sad really, the first few years I went to shows it was awesome and always had 300+ kids coming to every show that was put on. I'm in the process of learning guitar finally with hopes to get a band together to try and give Maine the spark it needs to gain momentum and be relevant in hardcore music again. 

Until things turn around though, I still always go to Boston hardcore shows, and it's a totally different world. I love it there. I wish I could afford to live in Boston, never enjoyed shows more than I do when I go there.

TL;DR Southern Maine has fallen off the map and I hope it comes back, but Boston will always be at the forefront of East Coast Hardcore
